lead: American painter and printmaker (1844-1926) who lived in Paris and showed with the Impressionists; known for soft pastels and flat color.
paras: Mary Cassatt was born near Pittsburgh, studied in Philadelphia, and settled in Paris in the 1870s. At Edgar Degas's invitation she joined the Impressionist group and showed with them in several of their exhibitions.

She worked in oil, pastel and printmaking. A large Japanese woodblock print exhibition in Paris in 1890 is widely credited with changing her approach, and her color prints that followed use flat areas and clear outlines.

Her pastels and oils are known for scenes of women and children, with pale skin and cloth set against soft green and blue grounds. Pastel keeps its color well, so the surfaces are closer to what she made than many oils of her time.
Compare a pastel with one of her color prints. The first blends colors by hand into a hazy field; the second sets a few colors down in separate flat shapes.

Our archive holds only 123 Cassatt paintings, so these findings are tentative. They are photographs of varnished or framed works, not measurements of pigment. She used very dark olive browns, Bistre and Café Noir about a third as often as her peers, and her darkest areas are Smoky Black and Black Blue. Her lightest are Tan, greyish white and Dawn Grey.
